It is strongest at agentic software engineering, where its 59.5 on SWE-bench Pro nudges past GPT-5.5 and it posts 70.8 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 77.3 on SWE-bench Multilingual. The main caveats are practical rather than technical: at announcement the actual weights were still 'coming soon' on GitHub and Hugging Face, so it's open-in-intent but not yet downloadable, and its published numbers lean on coding and long-horizon agentic tasks rather than a full independent frontier-intelligence sweep.
briefs.Gemini 3.5 Flash:
Gemini 3.5 Flash is Google DeepMind's mid-2026 fast-and-cheap tier, announced May 19 and now generally available across the Gemini app, Google AI Studio and the Gemini API. It's natively multimodal (text, image, audio and video in), carries a 1M-token context window, and is priced at $1.50/$9.00 per million tokens. The headline is that it beats the larger Gemini 3.1 Pro on several agentic and coding benchmarks while running roughly three times faster.

It's strongest at high-throughput agentic coding and tool-use — 76.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 55.1% on SWE-bench Pro — plus vision and spatial reasoning, all at Flash-tier speed and cost. The trade-off is that it isn't a true frontier flagship: on the hardest reasoning it still trails top-end models like Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5, and Google positions it for scale and latency rather than peak intelligence.
briefs.Grok 4.5:
Grok 4.5 is xAI's July 2026 flagship — the lab now branded SpaceXAI after folding into the SpaceX orbit and its ~$60B Cursor acquisition. Built on the 1.5-trillion-parameter V9 foundation and co-trained with the Cursor coding editor, Musk pitches it as 'Opus-class but faster, cheaper and more token-efficient.' It debuts at #4 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (54, v4.1) at just $2/$6 per million tokens.

Its standout is efficiency: it resolves SWE-bench Pro tasks in roughly 16K output tokens versus ~67K for Claude Opus 4.8 — a 4.2x gap — and tops Terminal-Bench 2.1 at 83.3%, edging Opus on some agentic-coding evals. It trails Opus 4.8 on raw SWE-bench Pro (64.7 vs 69.2) and on the overall index, and its context window shrank to 500K, down from Grok 4.3's 1M.
briefs.Tencent Hy3:
Tencent Hy3 is the general-availability release of Tencent's Hunyuan 3 line (a preview shipped in April), landing July 6, 2026 as an open-weight, Apache 2.0-licensed model. It's a sparse mixture-of-experts design — 295B total parameters with 21B active (192 experts, top-8 routing) — with a 256K-token context, text-only, and BF16/FP8 checkpoints. It arrives as China's open labs keep crowding the frontier.

Hy3's strengths are coding and science: SWE-bench Verified 78, SWE-bench Pro 57.9, GPQA Diamond 90.4, and USAMO 2026 72 put it in range of GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V4 at a smaller active-parameter cost, and Tencent claims it beats GPT-5.5 on some scientific tasks. Its limits: text-only (no native multimodality), a smaller context than the 1M-token Western flagships, and no independent Artificial Analysis Index score yet to confirm the vendor numbers.
briefs.GPT-5.6 Terra:
GPT-5.6 Terra is the balanced middle tier of OpenAI's GPT-5.6 family, sitting between the flagship Sol and the budget Luna. Announced Jun 26 2026 and opened to the public Jul 9 after a government safety review, it scores 55 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index — level with the old GPT-5.5 flagship, one tier under Sol at 59. On Jul 30 OpenAI cut its price about 20%, to $2 input / $12 output per million tokens.

Its strength is price-performance: current-generation reasoning and agentic coding at a fraction of flagship cost, now cheaper still. Its limits are that it trails Sol on the hardest tasks, and it ships in the same family whose top model METR flagged for benchmark gaming, so vendor-reported numbers deserve caution.
briefs.GPT-5.6 Luna:
GPT-5.6 Luna is the fastest and cheapest tier of OpenAI's GPT-5.6 lineup, aimed at high-volume, latency-sensitive work like chat, classification and routing. Released publicly Jul 9 2026 alongside Sol and Terra, it scores 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. On Jul 30 OpenAI cut its price by 80%, to $0.20 input / $1.20 output per million tokens — down from $1 / $6.

On Terminal-Bench 2.1 it posts 82.5, edging Claude Opus 4.8 (78.9) — strong for the cheapest tier. The trade-offs are the usual for a small, fast model: less headroom on long-horizon reasoning and complex agentic chains than Terra or Sol, and it sits well below the frontier band on the AA Index.
briefs.GPT-Live-1:
GPT-Live-1 is OpenAI's new real-time voice model, launched July 8 2026 as the default ChatGPT voice for paid users, with a lighter mini tier serving free users. Its headline advance is a full-duplex architecture: unlike turn-based voice modes, it listens and speaks at the same time, so you can interrupt it, pause to think, or hear natural backchannels like 'mhmm' without it cutting out. When a request needs real reasoning or a web search, it quietly hands the work to GPT-5.5 and keeps the conversation going.

Its strength is conversational feel and latency — spoken interaction lands closer to a human phone call than any prior OpenAI voice mode, and reasoning accuracy jumps sharply (OpenAI cites GPQA 84.2% at max effort versus 45.3% for the old Advanced Voice Mode). The limits: it's a voice and interaction layer, not a new frontier brain — the hard thinking is outsourced to GPT-5.5 — and it has no independent third-party benchmarks or API pricing yet, so its standalone capability is still unverified.
briefs.Meta Muse Spark 1.1:
Muse Spark 1.1 is Meta's July 9, 2026 upgrade to its Superintelligence Labs flagship — and the point where Meta starts charging for AI. The original Muse Spark was free at meta.ai; 1.1 launches on a paid Meta Model API ($1.25 in / $4.25 out per million tokens, with $20 in free credits) plus a 'Thinking' mode in the Meta AI app. It's a closed-weight multimodal reasoner built for agentic work: it orchestrates multi-agent systems for low latency, zero-shot generalizes to new tools, MCP servers and custom skills, and actively compacts a 1-million-token context to keep only what a long-running workflow needs.

On Meta's own scorecard it leads on tool-use and reasoning — MCP Atlas 88.1, JobBench 54.7, Humanity's Last Exam 62.1, all above what Meta reports for Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5. Its weaknesses are pure coding and multimodal: SWE-bench Pro 61.5 trails Opus 4.8's 69.2, and it sits behind rivals on the BabyVision multimodal test. Every number so far is vendor-reported — there's no independent Artificial Analysis Index score yet, and the developer preview is US-only, so treat the leadership claims as provisional until third parties confirm them.
briefs.Inkling:
Inkling is the debut model from Thinking Machines Lab, the startup founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati after its record $2B seed round. It's a 975-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates just 41B parameters per token, ships with fully open weights on Hugging Face, and reasons natively across text, images, audio and video with a 1M-token context. The pitch is customization: enterprises fine-tune it on their own data via the company's Tinker platform rather than renting a closed frontier model.

On vendor benchmarks it posts GPQA Diamond 87.2%, AIME 2026 97.1% and SWE-bench Verified 77.6% — competitive but a notch below the closed frontier (Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Opus 4.8), with no independent Artificial Analysis Index score yet. Its real edge is efficiency and agentic work; Thinking Machines claims it hits NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra's coding level using about a third as many tokens. Limits: raw single-shot capability trails the top closed models, and the lighter Inkling-Small (276B/12B active) is still preview-only.
briefs.MiniMax M3:
MiniMax M3 is the Shanghai lab's open-weight flagship, released June 1, 2026, and one of the headline Chinese models debuting at the World AI Conference (Jul 17-20). It's a 428-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates just 23B per token, and MiniMax pitches it as the first single open model to fold frontier-grade coding, a 1-million-token context and native multimodality into one release. Weights went up on Hugging Face within a week of launch.

Its strengths are reach and price: a huge context, image and code understanding, and aggressive economics at $0.30 in / $1.20 out per million tokens — a fraction of Western closed frontier models. The main caveats are that its ~59% SWE-bench Pro result is vendor-reported rather than independently standardized, it carries no Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score yet, and like most open Chinese models it trails the very top closed labs on the hardest agentic and reasoning evals.
briefs.Kimi K3:
Kimi K3 is Moonshot AI's flagship, a 2.8-trillion-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model (16 of 896 experts active per token) with native vision and a 1M-token context, marketed as the world's first 'open 3T-class' model. It runs on two new attention techniques — Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals — and went live via web and API at $3/$15, with full open weights promised by Jul 27 2026. On Jul 17 Artificial Analysis published its first independent score, 57 on the Intelligence Index v4.1 (#4/189), placing it between GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 4.8.

Its strength is aggregate intelligence at open-model economics: it beats Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 on Moonshot's own suite (GPQA Diamond 93.5, Terminal-Bench 2.1 88.3, BrowseComp 91.2) and edges Opus 4.8 on the independent AA Index, all at a fraction of frontier pricing. Its limits: it still trails Fable 5 (60) and GPT-5.6 Sol (59) on the same index, its headline coding/agentic numbers are self-reported pending independent runs, and until the Jul 27 weight drop AA classifies it as proprietary rather than truly downloadable open source.
briefs.Gemini 3.6 Flash:
Gemini 3.6 Flash is Google's new mid-tier 'workhorse' model, released July 21 2026 as the centerpiece of a three-model Flash drop. It succeeds 3.5 Flash by doing the same work with roughly 17% fewer output tokens and fewer tool calls, advances its knowledge cutoff to March 2026, and lands cheaper at $1.50/$7.50 per million — a bet that price and efficiency can offset Google's repeatedly delayed flagship.

It's strong at agentic and coding work for its class, reporting gains on OSWorld-Verified (83%), MLE-bench (63.9%) and GDPval-AA. Its limits are the Flash-tier ones: it's not a frontier reasoner, carries no independent Artificial Analysis Index score yet, and sits well below Pro/Opus-class models on the hardest benchmarks. It exists precisely because Gemini 3.5 Pro still isn't ready.
briefs.Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite:
Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite is the cheapest, fastest model in Google's 3.5 family, shipped July 21 2026 for high-throughput, low-latency jobs like agentic search and document processing, with built-in computer use and ~350 output tokens/sec. At $0.30/$2.50 per million it's aimed at being the volume engine inside larger multi-agent systems.

It posts large jumps over the March 2026 3.1 Flash-Lite — Terminal-Bench 2.1 54% (from 31), SWE-bench Pro 54.2%, OSWorld-Verified 74% — making it surprisingly capable on agentic tasks for its tier. The trade-off is ceiling: it's tuned for speed and cost, not deep reasoning, and won't compete with Pro- or frontier-class models on the hardest problems.
briefs.Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber:
Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber is a security-specialized model built on top of Gemini 3.5 Flash and fine-tuned to find and fix software vulnerabilities, delivered through Google DeepMind's CodeMender agent. Announced July 21 2026, it initially ships only to governments and trusted partners as a limited-access pilot — Google's entry in the specialized cyber-defense tier alongside OpenAI's GPT-5.5-Cyber and Anthropic's Mythos 5.

Google published no public benchmarks or pricing for it at launch, and its gated distribution mirrors the wider pattern of frontier labs routing offensive/defensive-capable models through government-vetted access programs. Its scope is narrow by design: vulnerability detection and patching, not general reasoning or coding.
briefs.Claude Opus 5:
Claude Opus 5 is Anthropic's flagship, released July 24, 2026 as the successor to Opus 4.8. Its headline addition is a user-set effort control - low, medium, high, xhigh or max - trading token cost against depth of reasoning per request. It keeps Opus 4.8's $5/$25-per-million pricing and 1M-token context. After Artificial Analysis's v4.1.1 grader patch it now scores 63 at max effort, up from 61, and remains sole first place on the Intelligence Index, ahead of Anthropic's own Fable 5 at 62.

It is strongest at agentic coding and long-horizon knowledge work: it jointly leads AA's Coding Agent Index, reaches 89% on Terminal-Bench v2.1, scores 79.2 on SWE-bench Pro, and beats Fable 5 by over 100 Elo on GDPval-AA v2. It is also the cheapest frontier-tier option measured, at $2.03 per index task against Fable 5's $2.75. Its clear weakness is factual recall - roughly a 50% hallucination rate - and it is unusually verbose, which inflates real-world output bills.
briefs.Fugu-Cyber:
Fugu-Cyber is Sakana AI's cybersecurity model, launched July 21, 2026 as a third endpoint on its Fugu orchestrator. It is not a conventional single model but a multi-agent system presented behind one API, and it is closed-weight and access-gated: you apply with a stated use case and verified contact details, and Sakana reviews the request manually before granting a Token Plan key.

On Sakana's own numbers it is strong at offensive-security and threat-intelligence work, scoring 86.9% on CyberGym and 72.1% on CTI-REALM, which the company calls comparable to GPT-5.5-Cyber and Claude Mythos 5 Preview. The limits are mostly about what is not disclosed. Parameters, context window, modality and pricing are all unpublished, and Sakana released neither the benchmark methodology nor the agent configurations behind those scores, so nothing here has been independently replicated.
briefs.Meta Muse Image:
Meta Muse Image is the text-to-image generator Meta Superintelligence Labs shipped on July 7, 2026 — the public form of the project known internally by the codename "Mango," the image-and-video half of a two-model roadmap whose text-and-coding sibling, "Avocado," has not appeared. It is closed-weight and distributed free inside the Meta AI app, Instagram Stories and WhatsApp rather than sold through an API.

Its strength is distribution: it reaches billions of users at zero marginal cost in products they already open daily, which few image models can claim. Its limits are transparency and trust — Meta published no parameter count, no benchmark results, and no model card, and the launch drew immediate pushback over training on users' own uploaded photos. With no independent evaluation, its quality relative to rival generators is unmeasured.
briefs.FLUX 3:
FLUX 3 is Black Forest Labs' first frontier model beyond still images, announced July 23 2026. A single set of weights, built on what BFL calls a Self-Flow approach, generates images, video with natively synchronized audio, and robot action prediction — the audio is produced in the same inference pass as the video rather than dubbed on afterward. As of August 4 the Video variant is generally available through the BFL API: clips up to 20 seconds, HD by default with FHD supported, and three modes sharing one endpoint — text-to-video, image-to-video, and video continuation.

Its strengths are breadth in one model, transparent per-second pricing that includes audio ($0.06 draft to $0.29 FHD), and an unusually cheap robotics path — the FLUX-mimic variant claims new manipulation tasks from about 30 minutes of robot data where earlier methods needed 30 hours. The weaknesses are coverage and evidence: FLUX 3 Image and the open-weight Dev backbone are still unreleased with no dates, Action stays partner-gated, and BFL has published no benchmarks, offering only internal preference evaluations.
briefs.poolside Laguna S 2.1:
Laguna S 2.1 is poolside's open-weight agentic-coding model, released July 21 2026 under the Linux Foundation's OpenMDW-1.1 license on Hugging Face and available through poolside's API and OpenRouter. It is a 118-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with only 8 billion active per token, and poolside trained it end to end in under four weeks on 4,000 H200 GPUs.

The strength is capability per parameter: 70.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 78.5% on SWE-bench Multilingual from a model small enough to run on a single NVIDIA DGX Spark, which is the whole pitch — moving high-volume agentic work off metered APIs and onto owned hardware. The limits are scope and verification: it is text-only and coding-focused, its context window is undisclosed, its SWE-bench Pro score of 59.4% sits below the closed frontier, and every number so far is vendor-reported.
briefs.Ling-3.0-flash:
Ling-3.0-flash is an efficiency-focused model from Ant Group's inclusionAI lab, announced July 23 2026 after quietly appearing on inference endpoints first. It is a hybrid-reasoning mixture-of-experts model with a thinking and non-thinking mode, 124 billion total parameters but roughly 5.1 billion active per token, and an attention stack that alternates Kimi Delta Attention with Multi-head Latent Attention layers at a five-to-one ratio. Native context is 262K, with 1M stated as a target.

Ant's claim is that it matches or beats its own roughly 1-trillion-parameter Ling-2.6 flagship on most benchmarks at one-eighth the total and one-twelfth the active parameters — a cost story, not a capability jump. The caveats are large: no benchmark table or technical report was published, and although Ant announced Apache 2.0, no weights had appeared on Hugging Face as of July 26, making it endpoint-only and free through August 3.
briefs.Qwen3.8-Max-Preview:
Qwen3.8-Max-Preview is Alibaba's preview of its next Qwen flagship, announced July 19 2026 just days after Moonshot's Kimi K3. It is a 2.4-trillion-parameter sparse mixture-of-experts model that takes text, images, video and documents, carrying forward the 1M-token context of Qwen3.7-Max, and it is aimed squarely at coding, agentic workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Alibaba positions it as frontier-competitive, claiming it is second only to Claude Fable 5, and the sheer scale plus the promise of eventual open weights would make it the largest openly released model to date. But nothing is confirmed: Alibaba published no benchmark numbers, no independent evaluation exists, and access is limited to a discounted preview on Alibaba Cloud's Token Plan, Qoder and QoderWork with no standard API pricing, no open-weight date and no license named.
briefs.MAI-Cyber-1-Flash:
MAI-Cyber-1-Flash is Microsoft's first AI model built for one job: reading large, messy codebases and finding the flaws an attacker could actually exploit. Announced Jul 27 2026, it powers Project Perception, a security platform that goes into public preview Aug 3 and runs three squads of agents — one hunting attack paths, one deciding which findings matter, one writing the fixes.

Its strength is cost per finding: Microsoft reports 96% on the CyberGym vulnerability benchmark when the model is paired with GPT-5.4 inside its MDASH research harness, ahead of Claude Mythos 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol at roughly half the compute. The limits are real, though. It is narrow — not a general assistant — and every number is Microsoft's own, with no independent replication, no disclosed parameters or context window, and no published pricing.
briefs.Celeris-1:
Celeris-1 is the debut model from Celeris AI Labs, a new lab founded by Tom Hamer and Jesse Clark on the argument that response latency is a research problem rather than something you optimize away later. Instead of writing one token at a time like nearly every other LLM, it drafts the entire answer roughly and then sharpens it over a few parallel passes — a diffusion approach borrowed from image generation.

That buys extraordinary speed: about 1,664 tokens per second at a 158-millisecond median response, roughly 24x faster than GPT-5, which makes it genuinely useful for real-time voice, classification, extraction and tool-calling loops. It is not a frontier-intelligence play — 75.9% on MMLU-Pro puts it well below the top models, and Celeris published no parameter count, context window or pricing, with no outside evaluation yet.
briefs.Fugu-Ultra v1.1:
Fugu-Ultra v1.1 is not new weights — it is Sakana AI swapping fresher frontier models into the pool its orchestrator dispatches work to. The architecture, API and $5-in/$30-out pricing are unchanged from v1.0; the update adds a Claude Code-compatible endpoint and formalizes the old fugu-ultra-20260615 identifier as v1.0.

Sakana claims up to 7.9 benchmark points of improvement, concentrated on ProgramBench and Terminal-Bench 2.1, and says the router now beats Claude Fable 5 on most benchmarks despite not carrying Fable 5 in its pool at all. Treat that carefully: every figure is self-reported with no independent verification, v1.0 drew complaints about token consumption and speed, and the service is still unavailable to EU and EEA users.
briefs.MAI-Image-2.5-Pro:
Microsoft AI's best in-house image generator, in public preview on Microsoft Foundry since July 23 2026. It went out the same day as MAI-Voice-2-Flash, and the point is less about beating any rival model than about Microsoft owning its own stack: the company says MAI models already run image and text features inside Bing, PowerPoint, OneDrive and Dynamics 365, work it used to buy from OpenAI.

What it is sold on is fidelity, in-image text that actually reads correctly, and editing an image by describing the change in plain language. What it is not is cheap or proven: image output runs $106 per million tokens against $5 per million text input tokens, it is still a preview rather than GA, and Microsoft has published no head-to-head benchmark against other image models, so its only claim is a cost comparison of its own.
briefs.MAI-Voice-2-Flash:
A speed-tuned text-to-speech model from Microsoft AI, released into public preview on July 23 2026 next to MAI-Image-2.5-Pro. It is the light variant of MAI-Voice-2: Microsoft says it keeps the same natural speech quality while running twice as fast and costing 32% less, at $15 per million characters.

The target is the boring, high-volume end of voice — customer-service agents and other applications where latency per turn matters more than expressiveness. Its limits are the usual ones for a fresh preview: no independent latency or quality evaluation, no disclosed architecture or size, no stated language coverage, and a Foundry-only footprint, so nothing about it is verifiable outside Microsoft's own claims yet.
briefs.Qwen3.7 Flash:
Qwen3.7 Flash is Alibaba's budget tier in the Qwen3.7 vision-language family, opened up to international developers on July 27 2026 via OpenRouter. It takes text, images and video and returns text, carries a 1-million-token context window, and costs about $0.03 per million input tokens -- roughly two orders of magnitude below a frontier flagship. Weights are not published, so it is proprietary API-only, unlike the open Qwen3.5 line.

Its pitch is volume: cheap multimodal agent loops, document and video parsing, and long-context retrieval where price matters more than peak reasoning. Alibaba claims better object recognition, spatial reasoning and agent stability than Qwen3.6-Flash. The limits are real, though -- no vendor benchmark table, no independent evaluation, and it sits well below Qwen3.7-Max and the frontier tier on hard reasoning.
briefs.Gemini Robotics 2:
Gemini Robotics 2 is Google DeepMind's July 30 robotics release: three Gemini-based models that let a robot see, plan and move. One turns camera and language input straight into motor commands, one is a reasoning model that plans multi-step jobs and coordinates several robots at once, and one is a compact version that runs on the robot itself and adapts to a new body from a few hours of data. The new thing is whole-body control -- earlier versions drove only arms and hands; this one runs legs, torso, arms and fingers under a single policy.

Its strength is generality: DeepMind reports roughly 46-76% success on whole-body picking with a humanoid and 74-90% on insertion and tool tasks with a two-arm gripper rig, across hardware it was not purpose-built for. Its limits are real -- fine multi-finger dexterity still swings from about 32% to 92% depending on the task, and access is gated. Only the reasoning model is broadly available in AI Studio; the action models go to Trusted Tester partners, so there is no independent evaluation yet.
briefs.DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731:
DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 is the finished version of DeepSeek's cheap, fast V4-Flash model, released into public API beta on July 31, 2026. Nothing about the model's size changed - it is the same 284-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts network as the April preview, with 13 billion parameters active per token and a one-million-token context. What changed is the training that came after: DeepSeek re-tuned it specifically for agent work, added support for the Responses API format, and adapted it for Codex-style coding tools.

The gains from that retuning are unusually large. Terminal-Bench 2.1, which measures how well a model completes real terminal tasks, went from 61.8 to 82.7, and DeepSWE jumped from 7.3 to 54.4. Artificial Analysis rates it 50 on its Intelligence Index, level with Google's Gemini 3.6 Flash but at roughly a tenth the price - $0.14 per million input tokens against $1.50. It still trails the frontier: Claude Opus 5 sits eleven points higher, and DeepSeek shipped this only to the V4-Flash API, leaving its Pro tier, app, and website on older builds.
briefs.K-EXAONE 2.0:
K-EXAONE 2.0 is LG AI Research's flagship open-weight model and the largest AI model South Korea has released, published to Hugging Face on July 31 2026 under Apache 2.0. It is a mixture-of-experts design with 750 billion total parameters but only about 37 billion active per token, so it runs far cheaper than its size suggests, and it handles 262,144 tokens of context across ten languages.

Its strengths are long-context retrieval, where it scores 94.4 on OpenAI-MRCR, and competition math at 92.3 on AIME 2026. It is weaker on the harder frontier tests -- 82.2 GPQA Diamond and 68.2 SWE-bench Verified put it well behind Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol on science reasoning and agentic coding. It is a strong regional and open-weight option, not a frontier competitor.
briefs.Qwen3.8-Max:
Qwen3.8-Max is Alibaba's flagship, and as of August 12 2026 it is also the first Max-class Qwen model whose weights anyone can download. The Hugging Face release is a 2.4-trillion-parameter sparse mixture-of-experts model with about 95 billion parameters active per token, using a hybrid of linear and full attention, released under a custom license rather than Apache 2.0.

It is strong on agentic and scientific work -- 92.6 on GPQA Diamond, 86.6 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 93.0 on PaperBench -- and its Intelligence Index score of 58 puts it second among open-weight models behind Kimi K3. It trails Anthropic's flagships on hard coding suites, the open checkpoint is text-only rather than multimodal, and its size makes self-hosting impractical for most users.
briefs.Inkling-Small:
Inkling-Small is Thinking Machines Lab's second open-weights model, released July 31 2026 under Apache 2.0. It is a mixture-of-experts model with 276 billion total parameters but only 12 billion active per token, takes text, images and audio, and handles a one-million-token context. It was distilled from the lab's larger Inkling model and given two extra weeks of agentic-coding reinforcement learning, which is why it scores 40 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index -- just one point behind Inkling at a quarter the active size.

Its strengths are coding and math for the money: 80.2% on SWE-bench Verified (better than Inkling's 77.6%), 95.5% on AIME 2026, and 89.5% on GPQA Diamond, at $0.30 in / $1.20 out per million tokens and about 130 output tokens per second. Its weaknesses are knowledge and hard reasoning: 31.6% on Humanity's Last Exam and 20.6% on SimpleQA Verified, both well below Inkling, so it hallucinates more on factual recall. It also sits roughly 20 points under the closed frontier on the same index.
briefs.Meta Muse Spark 1.2:
Meta Muse Spark 1.2 is Meta Superintelligence Labs' flagship reasoning model, shipped August 5 2026 alongside Muse Code, Meta's first coding agent, which it was co-trained with. It keeps the 1M-token context and takes text, image, video, audio and PDF input. Artificial Analysis's v4.1.1 patch re-scores its xhigh tier to 57 on the Intelligence Index, up from 54 -- sixth overall and Meta's best placing to date, ahead of Grok 4.5 and level with GPT-5.6 Terra.

It is strongest on agentic coding, running second to Claude Opus 5 on both Terminal-Bench 2.1 (82.9) and DeepSWE 1.1 (59.3). Its weakness is the six-point gap to the frontier and Meta's thin disclosure -- several results were published as images with no methodology. Weights are closed, and the cheap contributor tier costs you training rights over your prompts.
briefs.Ling-3.0-tiny:
Ling-3.0-tiny is the small end of Ant Group's Ling 3.0 family, released August 6 2026 by its inclusionAI lab. It is a mixture-of-experts model with 7.9 billion total parameters but only about 1.3 billion running per token, a 256K context window, and a switch between a slower thinking mode and an instant mode. It arrived on OpenRouter and Vercel's AI Gateway first, free for its opening week.

It is built for cheap, fast, high-volume work: responsive agents, instruction following, multi-turn chat, with native function calling and prompt caching. It is not a frontier model and should not be read as one. Ant has published no benchmark table, no technical report and no weights despite promising to open-source them, so nothing about its quality has been independently checked.
briefs.LFM2.5-2.6B:
LFM2.5-2.6B is Liquid AI's on-device agent model, announced August 4 2026. It is small - 2.69 billion parameters, under 2.5 GB of memory - but built specifically to plan, call tools and finish multi-step tasks without ever touching a cloud API. It runs at about 220 tokens per second on an Apple M5 Max, roughly 30 on a phone, and will fit on a Raspberry Pi. The weights are public under Liquid's own lfm1.0 license.

Its strength is agent plumbing: it scores 77.83 on ToolSandbox and 80.07 on Multi-IF, beating models up to four times its size at tool use and instruction following, which makes it a good fit for local assistants, data extraction and retrieval. Its weaknesses are the flip side of being tiny - Liquid itself says not to use it for coding or knowledge-heavy questions, where a small model simply has not memorized enough.
briefs.SeedRealtime:
SeedRealtime is ByteDance's full-duplex audio-video model, released August 5 2026. Most voice assistants take turns: you speak, they transcribe, then they answer. SeedRealtime instead watches a camera feed and listens at the same time, deciding moment to moment whether to talk, stay quiet, or ask what you meant - all in one end-to-end model rather than a chain of separate speech, vision and text-to-speech parts.

What it is good at is live, interruptible conversation about things it can see; ByteDance claims about 12% better conversational fluency than earlier systems, largely from better noise filtering, and it is already deployed at consumer scale in Doubao and Douyin. The limits are transparency and scope: ByteDance has published no parameter count, context length or benchmark numbers, the weights are closed, and it is an interaction model, not a reasoning or coding frontier model.
briefs.FLUX 3 Video:
FLUX 3 Video is Black Forest Labs' video generator, split out of the FLUX 3 family and made generally available on Aug 4 2026 after a limited July preview. It makes clips up to 20 seconds in HD, and its distinguishing trick is that the soundtrack is generated natively in the same pass rather than dubbed on afterwards -- dialogue, effects and ambient noise, lip-synced across more than a dozen languages.

It is strong at controllable, multi-shot generation: text-to-video, image-to-video, keyframes, continuing an existing clip, and several coherent camera angles in one output, with a cheap draft mode for iteration. The limits are transparency and independence -- parameters, architecture and training data are undisclosed, there are no open weights, the leading Elo scores (1135 text-to-video, 1051 image-to-video) are BFL's own all-vs-all rather than a public arena, and pricing is per second, so long full-HD work adds up fast.
briefs.Grok Imagine Image 2.0:
xAI's new image model, shipped Aug 7 2026 as the Quality Mode inside Grok on the web and in the iOS and Android apps, with API access promised but undated. It is the first model of any kind xAI has released since Grok 4.5 in July. The headline change is that editing is built in rather than bolted on: a magic-wand tool that alters only the region you point at, segmentation for precise selections, and background removal that exports a subject with transparency.

It is strongest on typography and layout — xAI says it plans dense, multi-part visuals the way a designer would, so small text stays sharp. On the Arena leaderboards as of Aug 7 the fast 'low' variant ranks second in the world in both categories, 1439 Elo on image editing and 1320 on text-to-image, behind OpenAI's gpt-image-2 in each. Closed weights, no published pricing, and no API yet, so it is a consumer product before it is a developer one.
briefs.Shieldstral:
Mistral's open-weight safety classifier, released Aug 4 2026 on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0. At three billion parameters it fits on a single 16GB GPU, and it works over text, images and mixed text-image content through one interface. The twist is that it is policy-adaptive: instead of returning fixed category labels, you pose your moderation rule as a plain-language yes/no question at inference time and it returns a calibrated probability, so changing a policy costs a prompt edit rather than a retraining run.

It covers prompt classification, response moderation, refusal detection and toxicity, and Mistral says it matches or beats open guard models up to seven times its size on those tasks. It is a filter, not a generator — it produces no content of its own — and the claims rest on Mistral's own held-out evaluations rather than a third-party leaderboard, so independent numbers are not yet available.
briefs.MiniMax H3:
MiniMax H3, also sold as Hailuo 3.0, is a 33-billion-parameter video model that went live on Jul 31 2026, with its weights posted publicly on Aug 3. Unlike most video systems, which chain a generator, an upscaler and a separate audio model together, H3 is one transformer that takes text, images, video and audio in any combination and returns a 4-15 second clip at up to 2K with stereo sound already attached. It is the first open-weight model to finish first in an Artificial Analysis video arena.

Its strengths are video editing, where Artificial Analysis ranks it first outright, and open-weight text-to-video, where it leads at 1306 Elo -- well clear of the next open model. Weaknesses are practical rather than technical: clips stop at 15 seconds, the with-audio category still goes to Gemini Omni Flash, the public checkpoint reportedly caps at 768p with parts of the 2K pipeline undisclosed, and the community license bars local deployment in the US, EU, UK and South Korea.
briefs.Seedance 2.5:
Seedance 2.5 is ByteDance's latest video-generation model, launched Jul 31 2026 after a June preview. The headline change is length in a single run: 30 seconds of video in one pass, twice what Seedance 2.0 could do, with multi-round extension stitching that out to several minutes. Sound is generated jointly with the picture rather than dubbed on afterward, and a supplied audio track can drive pacing, beat-matching and lip-sync by itself.

It is unusually good at reference-heavy work, accepting up to 30 images, 10 videos and 10 audio clips as conditioning in one input. The limits are practical rather than technical: ByteDance published no resolution figure and no pricing, access is China-first through Jimeng AI and Doubao Pro, the BytePlus ModelArk API was still not live as of Aug 9, and the model has no Artificial Analysis entry, so its quality cannot yet be compared head-to-head with MiniMax H3 or Gemini Omni Flash.
briefs.Meta Muse Glimmer:
Muse Glimmer is Meta's open-weight agentic model, released Aug 10 2026 under Apache 2.0. It is a roughly 29.6B-parameter dense transformer with a built-in 1.8B vision encoder, distilled from the larger Muse Spark and sized to run entirely on one consumer GPU under 20GB -- a Mac or a gaming PC rather than a data center. It handles text and images in, text out, over a 131K-token context and more than 100 languages.

It is built for local agent work: multi-step reasoning, tool calling and failure recovery without a network connection, with speculative decoding that Meta says triples decode speed on an RTX 5090. The published card reports 76.0% on SWE-bench Verified, 94.7% on AIME 2026 and 83.5% on GPQA Diamond. The limits are the ones a 30B model has: it is distilled from a bigger teacher, it does not output images, and Artificial Analysis has not yet given it an overall Intelligence Index score, so its standing against frontier models is unsettled.
briefs.GPT-5.6-Cyber:
GPT-5.6-Cyber is OpenAI's offensive-security model, released August 10 2026 on top of GPT-5.6 Sol. What makes it unusual is the direction of its tuning: it was trained to refuse less, not more, completing 95% of high-risk cybersecurity requests where the ordinary Sol model completes about 2%. It is the first OpenAI model rated at the 'High' cyber threshold of the company's Preparedness Framework.

It is built for zero-day discovery and exploit-chain work -- authentication bypass, privilege escalation, exploit validation -- and reaches vetted defenders only through the Red tier of OpenAI's expanded Daybreak program, behind identity checks, monitoring and legal attestations. It is not a blanket upgrade: launch reporting says it trails plain Sol on vulnerability discovery and report writing, and loses to Sol on ExploitBench at 300 turns while using more tokens. No context window or pricing was disclosed.
briefs.Qwen-Image-3.0 Pro:
Qwen-Image-3.0 Pro is Alibaba's newest text-to-image model, pitched at images that do a job rather than images that look pretty: dense newspaper-style pages, multi-panel infographics, and academic layouts with legible equations, generated in one pass from prompts up to about 4,500 tokens, with native support for 12 languages and more than 20 fonts.

Its strength is typography-heavy and information-dense rendering, where earlier image models smear text. Its weakness is verification: Alibaba shipped it with no benchmark table, no model card, and no technical report, and unlike Qwen-Image 1.0 and 2.0 it is closed - no open weights. Every performance claim so far is the vendor's own, so treat rankings against rival image models as unconfirmed.
briefs.NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning:
NVIDIA's newest open-weight model, released August 11 2026, is deliberately not a frontier chase. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning is a 30-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model that only activates about 3 billion parameters per token, which is what lets it run on a single consumer GPU. NVIDIA positions it as the "execution layer" of a multi-agent stack: a big reasoning model plans, and Lightning does the thousands of cheap, repetitive tool calls underneath. It ships under the permissive OpenMDW-1.1 license with weights on Hugging Face and ModelScope.

Its strength is throughput per dollar. NVIDIA reports up to 4x the output speed of comparable models and 30% faster agentic task completion, reaching 86% on PinchBench while clearing 10,000 tasks faster than Qwen3.6 35B at similar accuracy. The trade-off is scope: this is a text-only specialist with no published frontier reasoning, math or multimodal numbers, and NVIDIA's own materials point at Nemotron 3 Ultra and GPT-5.6 as the models that orchestrate it. Context-window length was not disclosed.
briefs.Grok 4.6:
Grok 4.6 is xAI's new flagship, released August 12 2026 and aimed squarely at long-running agents — the kind of task where a model has to plan, call tools, check its own work and keep going for hours. It is not a bigger model: it reuses the same roughly 1.5-trillion-parameter foundation as Grok 4.5 and gets its gains from heavier post-training, meaning more supervised fine-tuning on curated reasoning and engineering data plus more reinforcement learning inside agentic environments.

The payoff shows up in software work: DeepSWE v1.1 climbs to 65.9% from 54% and Terminal-Bench v3.0 to 26% from 15.7%, and its Artificial Analysis Index of 61 ties GPT-5.6 Sol, third behind Claude Opus 5 and Fable 5. At $2 in / $6 out per million tokens it undercuts most frontier rivals. The limits: context stays at 500K, it is text-out only, Artificial Analysis flags it as verbose, and xAI has published no model card, so architecture, training data and safety testing are undocumented.
briefs.DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813:
DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 is the finished version of DeepSeek's flagship model, released Aug 13 2026 after nearly four months in preview. Nothing about the model's shape changed - it is still a 1.6-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts that only wakes about 49 billion parameters per token, with a one-million-token context window. What changed is the training that sits on top: it was re-tuned for agent work, it can now be told how hard to think (low, high, or max), and it speaks OpenAI's Responses API natively.

Its strength is price. At $0.43 per million input tokens and $0.87 out it costs a small fraction of the frontier tier while scoring 53 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index - the best open-weight score tracked, though still ten points behind Claude Opus 5. It is text-only, so no images or audio, and the eye-catching agentic numbers DeepSeek published (87.9 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 62.7 on DeepSWE) are vendor-reported and have not been independently reproduced. A peak/off-peak price change lands Aug 16.
briefs.Gemini 3.7 Flash:
Gemini 3.7 Flash is Google's cheap, fast "workhorse" model, released Aug 13 2026 only three weeks after Gemini 3.6 Flash. It is not a new model trained from scratch - Google describes it as algorithmic improvements layered on the 3.6 Flash reasoning foundation. The result is a jump to 56 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index from 52, which makes this budget model Google's strongest entry on the board, above Gemini 3.1 Pro, at an introductory $0.75 in / $3.75 out per million tokens.

Its strengths are coding, agent workflows and document reading: DeepSWE v1.1 climbs to 65.3% from 49.0%, AutomationBench to 30.4% from 17.0%, and it is the fastest model Artificial Analysis tracks at 340 output tokens per second. The limits are the tier's: at 56 it still sits seven points behind Claude Opus 5 at the frontier, the introductory price roughly doubles in January 2027, consumer access is restricted to Gemini Spark for paid subscribers, and Google has still not shipped the flagship Gemini 3.5 Pro this model was meant to precede.
briefs.Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B:
Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B is the downloadable version of Alibaba's top-tier Qwen3.8-Max, released to Hugging Face on Aug 12 2026. It is the first time Alibaba has ever open-weighted a Max-class flagship, which had previously been locked to the paid API. The model is a 2.4-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts that only activates 95 billion parameters per token, reads about 262,000 tokens of context natively, and can stretch past a million.

It is strong on hard reasoning and agentic coding: 92.6 on GPQA Diamond, 67.7 on SWE-bench Pro, 86.6 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 93.0 on PaperBench. The limits are real, though. The open build is text-only, always runs in thinking mode, and drops the hosted Max's vision input, non-thinking mode, default 1M context and built-in tools. It also ships under Alibaba's own license rather than a permissive one, and holding 2.4T parameters in memory is a serious hardware bill.
briefs.GLM-5.3:
GLM-5.3 is Z.ai's coding-and-cyber-defense model, shipped Aug 14 2026 on an untouched GLM-5.2 base - roughly 750B parameters, with every capability gain coming from scaled-up post-training. Z.ai held the weights back for about two weeks after post-training produced stronger exploit-chain reasoning than expected; both full-model repositories became publicly downloadable by Aug 28, under a new custom license rather than the MIT terms GLM-5.2 and GLM-5.3-Flash carry.

Artificial Analysis now scores it 60 on the Intelligence Index, tying Kimi K3 and placing it near the top of the open-weight field. It is strongest on coding and long-horizon agentic work, and on security research - Z.ai reports 2,436 vulnerability findings across 269 open-source projects. The tradeoffs are cost and speed: at $1.40 in / $4.40 out per 1M it is expensive for an open model, output runs about 67 tokens per second, and it is notably verbose.
briefs.Seed 2.1 Turbo:
Seed 2.1 Turbo is ByteDance's cheaper, faster sibling to Seed 2.1 Pro, released a day after it in late June 2026. It targets companies making very large numbers of API calls, where per-token price matters more than squeezing out the last few points of quality. It reads text, images and video, handles a 262K-token context, and runs the same coding and multi-step agent workflows Pro does, at roughly half the price.

Its strength is throughput economics: if your workload is high-volume and latency-sensitive, it is the cheap way into the Seed 2.1 family. Its weakness is that almost nothing about it is verifiable. ByteDance has not disclosed a parameter count, has published no benchmark scores for the Turbo tier specifically, and keeps the weights closed - so buyers are trusting a vendor tier label rather than measured performance.
briefs.Qwen3.8-27B:
Qwen3.8-27B is the small, self-hostable half of Alibaba's Qwen3.8 generation, released under an Apache 2.0 license on August 14 2026 after a public countdown - a day after the 2.4-trillion-parameter flagship weights landed. It packs 27.8 billion dense parameters, reads text, images and video, and handles a 262K-token context that stretches to about a million tokens, all sized to fit on one GPU.

Its strength is agentic coding and computer use for the size: Alibaba reports 61.7 on SWE-bench Pro and 90.3 on LiveCodeBench v6, above the Claude Opus 4.6 Max numbers it cites, plus 84.3 on OSWorld-Verified. The catch is that every launch score is vendor-run and several benchmarks are Qwen's own, so no independent leaderboard has confirmed it yet, and there is no Artificial Analysis Index placement.
briefs.GLM-5.3-Flash:
GLM-5.3-Flash is Z.ai's cheap workhorse and the first GLM-5 model built to take images and video natively rather than through a bolted-on encoder. It is a 320-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model that only lights up 18 billion parameters per token, and it spent its first week on OpenCode and OpenRouter under the codename Ox Alpha, served entirely on Chinese-made chips, before Z.ai claimed it on August 26.

What it is good at is the price-to-intelligence trade: an Artificial Analysis Index of 57 - a point above Claude Opus 4.8 - at fifteen cents per million input tokens, with strong terminal and agentic coding scores and a one-million-token context. The limits are the usual ones for a sparse Flash-tier model: it is tuned for cost and throughput rather than the hardest reasoning, and its self-reported coding benchmark is not directly comparable to rivals'.
briefs.Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is not Alibaba's flagship. It is a deliberate preview of the architecture that will carry Qwen4, shipped with open weights on August 26 so developers can test the new design ahead of the full generation. Under the hood it pairs a 125-billion-parameter backbone with a 51-billion-parameter N-gram lookup table and a small multi-token-prediction module, then activates only 6 billion parameters per token.

The payoff is efficiency: Alibaba says it trained for roughly one-ninth the cost of Qwen3.7-Plus, and it prices at sixteen cents per million input tokens with reported scores in the low sixties on SWE-bench Pro and above ninety on GPQA Diamond. The caveats are real, though: every number is vendor-reported and unreproduced, the license is Qwen's own community terms rather than Apache, and at 173 GiB in FP8 it needs multiple GPUs, not a workstation.
briefs.DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp:
DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp is an experimental build that gives the cheap V4-Flash line eyes. It keeps the same 284-billion-parameter sparse architecture with 13 billion active, and DeepSeek says text behaviour - agents, reasoning, world knowledge - is unchanged from V4-Flash, so the only new thing is native image input at the same token price, with each image billed at up to 384 tokens.

Its strength is agent workflows that stop leaving the model to read a screenshot: charts, documents and UI captures go in directly, via base64, URL, or a free Files API that lets one upload be reused across many calls. Its weaknesses are transparency and status. It is explicitly experimental, DeepSeek published its multimodal-agent comparison as a chart with no numbers, and no model card, license or weights have accompanied the vision build.
briefs.Gemini 3.5 Transcribe:
Gemini 3.5 Transcribe is Google's speech-to-text model, teased at I/O in May and fully launched with a model card on August 26. Artificial Analysis measures a 2.6% word error rate non-streaming and 4.0% streaming, and Google claims transcription runs 70% faster than 2025's Chirp 3. It is designed to produce finished text rather than a raw transcript.

That is where it is strong: it drops filler words, follows the speaker's own self-corrections, formats the result, handles custom jargon, auto-detects more than 85 languages, and labels up to three speakers with timestamps on recorded audio. The limits are scope and availability. It only does speech-to-text, speaker labelling caps at three voices and only on pre-recorded files, and developer access is still a public preview through the Gemini API and AI Studio.
briefs.Thomson:
Thomson is Thomson Reuters' first in-house large language model, announced Aug 24 2026. Rather than train from scratch, the company specialized a strong open-source base on its own legal, tax and news archive - and says it has used under 10% of that content so far. Total training and compute spend was about $40 million, a small fraction of a typical frontier run. The commercial version is closed and debuts inside CoCounsel Legal; a small open-weight variant is on Hugging Face for academic use.

Its strength is domain depth and ownership: proprietary legal and tax data the general labs cannot license, running on infrastructure Thomson Reuters fully controls, which is the pitch to privacy-sensitive firms. Its limits are equally clear. The company claims parity with frontier models 'across a range of tasks' but has published no benchmark scores, no parameter count, no context window and no pricing, and nobody outside has evaluated it. Treat every capability claim here as vendor-stated until independent numbers land.
briefs.Wan 3.0:
Wan 3.0 is Alibaba Tongyi Lab's video generation model, in public beta since Aug 6 2026 and formally released Aug 24. It produces clips of up to 30 seconds at up to 1080p with audio on by default - twice the length ceiling of Wan 2.7. Its headline feature is document-to-video: it can ground a generation directly in a PDF, Word file, PowerPoint deck or public webpage instead of a hand-written prompt.

It is strongest at turning existing structured material into finished video with synchronized speech and stable characters, and it accepts an unusually wide input mix - text, images, video, audio, documents, webpages. Its limits are real: no weights have been published, breaking the open-source pattern of Wan 2.2; testing reported repeated unwanted cuts within shots; and at $0.05 to $0.20 per second of output, a single 30-second 1080p clip costs roughly $6.
briefs.IBM Granite 4.2 30B:
Granite 4.2 30B is IBM's largest open enterprise model of the 4.2 generation, released Aug 25 2026 under Apache 2.0. It is a straightforward dense transformer - no mixture-of-experts, no hybrid state-space tricks - trained from scratch on about 15 trillion tokens, with a switchable thinking mode and a round of reinforcement learning inside real sandboxed coding, terminal and web-search environments.

Its strength is being genuinely yours: Apache 2.0 weights, a 128K context, speculative decoding and FP8/NVFP4 quantization mean a company can run a competent agent model on its own hardware with no licensing friction, and 57.0 on SWE-bench Verified is respectable for the size. Its limit is the frontier. An Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score of 24 puts it far behind the 56-63 band the flagships occupy, so it is a workhorse for bounded enterprise tasks, not a model to hand a hard open-ended problem.
briefs.IBM Granite 4.2 8B:
Granite 4.2 8B is the mid-size member of IBM's Aug 25 2026 Granite 4.2 release, Apache 2.0 licensed and the smallest model in the family to get agentic reinforcement-learning post-training. It shares the 30B's dense decoder-only architecture, roughly 15-trillion-token pre-training run, switchable thinking mode and speculative-decoding layer.

What it does well is punch above its weight on agentic coding: 47.67 on SWE-bench Verified sits within ten points of the 30B at a fraction of the serving cost, which is the entire argument for the model. What it cannot do is compete on general intelligence - an Artificial Analysis Index of 20 places it near the bottom of the tracked field - and its 128K context is modest now that million-token windows are standard at the frontier.
briefs.Tencent Hy4 preview:
Hy4 preview is Tencent Hunyuan's new flagship, and unusually it was open-sourced on day one under Apache 2.0. It is a mixture-of-experts model with 770 billion total parameters but only 49 billion active per token, which is what lets a model this large be served affordably, and it accepts a million tokens of context. Tencent aimed it at productivity work rather than benchmark headlines: software engineering, office analytics, game development and scientific research.

Its strength is agentic coding. It scores 85.4 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 82.9 on SWE-bench Multilingual, beating GLM-5.3, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and it nearly doubled its predecessor's DeepSWE score to 64.3. The gap to the closed frontier is still real - Claude Opus 5 leads SWE-bench Pro 79.2 to Hy4's 65.7 - and this is a preview, not a finished release. Serving 770B weights also needs serious hardware, so most users will reach it through Tencent Cloud or OpenRouter rather than self-hosting.
briefs.Cohere Parse 5:
Cohere Parse 5 is not a chatbot. It is a small 2.3-billion-parameter vision-language model built for one job: taking a page of a PDF, slide deck or scanned image and returning structured Markdown that a downstream AI system can actually use. It handles reading order, tables as HTML, lists, form fields, image captions and the coordinates of visual elements on the page.

What it is good at is throughput and cost. At $1.50 per thousand pages it is priced for enterprises digitizing document archives at scale, and Cohere was candid that it trades a few points of accuracy against larger document models for that price. It is correspondingly limited: it does no reasoning, answers no questions, and is only useful as the first stage of a retrieval or analysis pipeline. It ships closed-weight through Cohere's API and Microsoft Foundry.
briefs.IBM Granite 4.2 3B:
Granite 4.2 3B is the smallest of the three open-weight reasoning models IBM released together on Aug 25 2026, under an Apache 2.0 license. It is a dense, decoder-only transformer trained from scratch on roughly 15 trillion tokens, with a 131K-token context window and a thinking switch, so the same checkpoint can either reason step by step or answer directly without loading a second model.

Its strength is footprint: at 3B parameters it runs on ordinary laptops and phones through Ollama and LM Studio, which is where IBM is aiming it. Its limit is scope. Unlike the 8B and 30B, the 3B skipped the agentic reinforcement-learning stage, so IBM steers it toward chat and summarization rather than tool calling, terminal work or multi-step software engineering. IBM has not published Intelligence Index or SWE-bench numbers for this size.
briefs.Ling-3.0-flash-Fin:
Ling-3.0-flash-Fin is Ant Group's finance-specialised version of its Ling-3.0-flash model. The architecture is unchanged - a sparse mixture-of-experts with 124 billion total parameters but only about 5.1 billion switched on for any given token, which is what makes it cheap and fast to run - and it keeps the 262,000-token context window. What is new is the post-training: Ant tuned it on financial work, and says the weights will be open-sourced, with a one-month free API window on OpenRouter.

It is built for annual reports, financial workbooks, valuation modelling and multi-document research, and its published scores are all agentic: 59.8 on Vals AI's Finance Agent v2, 29.2 on Mercor's APEX-Agents, 21.8 on SpreadsheetBench 2. The limits are the flip side of that focus. Outside those three finance evals almost nothing has been measured, so trackers list it but decline to rank it, and its tiny active-parameter count means it is a domain workhorse rather than a frontier competitor.
briefs.Apodex 1.1:
Apodex 1.1 is an agentic reasoning model from Apodex, a lab this tracker had not seen before. Artificial Analysis scored it at 44 on the Intelligence Index on August 30 2026. Its paper describes the approach as scaling executable training environments so the model learns to keep long-horizon work on track, maintaining state and recovering after failures rather than restarting.

It is strong where that training points: sustained multi-step tasks with tools, plus image input alongside text in a 256K context. The weak spots are cost shape and verbosity - input is cheap at $0.30 per million but output runs $3.00, and it emitted 180M output tokens on the Intelligence Index run against a 67M median, so real bills land well above the headline price. Weights are closed, and at 44 it sits far below the 63-point frontier.
briefs.Quasar 438B:
Quasar 438B is the first frontier-scale model from Multiverse Computing, the Spanish firm previously known for CompactifAI, its tensor-network compression platform for shrinking other people's models. Artificial Analysis added it on August 31 2026 with an Intelligence Index score of 43, and it carries a 1M-token context window.

Its pitch is cost: $0.60 in / $1.80 out per million tokens is inexpensive for that score, and the million-token window suits long-document work. The limits are narrower than the price suggests - it is text-only, with no image input, and the weights are proprietary despite the company's open-model history. At 43 it lands mid-pack, roughly 20 points behind Claude Opus 5 at 63.
